blocks.text: **The problem.** Given an `m × n` binary matrix of `"0"`s and `"1"`s, find the largest **square** made only of 1s and return its **area**.

blocks.alt: The matrix 1010 / 1111 / 1111 / 1011 and its table side[r][c], the side of the largest all-ones square whose bottom-right corner is at r, c. A cell holding 1 takes 1 plus the smallest of its left, upper and upper-left neighbours: side[2][2] = 1 + min(2, 1, 1) = 2. The largest side is 2, so the area is 4.

elements.text: side[r][c] = 1 + min(left, above, above-left) when the cell is 1
elements.originalText: side[r][c] = 1 + min(left, above, above-left) when the cell is 1

blocks.text: The idea: the square ending at each cell

Let `side[r][c]` be the side of the largest all-ones square whose **bottom-right corner** is `(r, c)`. If the cell is 0, it's 0. If it's 1, the square can grow only as far as its three neighbours allow — the squares ending to the **left**, **above** and **above-left** each limit it — so `side[r][c] = 1 + min(left, above, above-left)`. The answer is the largest side anywhere, squared.
1. Grow a square from every corner
**Time O(m · n · min(m, n)²), space O(1).** Each corner grows its square one ring at a time.

blocks.caption: Each 1 extends the smallest of the three squares touching it.

blocks.text: **Time O(m · n), space O(m · n)** — or O(n) with one row plus a variable remembering the old above-left value. Why the minimum? A square of side s at (r, c) needs squares of side s − 1 ending at all three neighbours; the smallest neighbour is the limit.
